mainTopic: Returning found documents (a גט, a שטר חוב, a bill of freedom, wills and gifts) when an early written date or a change of mind could cause harm.
overview: The amud opens with the end of a story. A גט that רבה בר בר חנה was carrying got lost in the בית מדרש and was returned to him. He then admitted he did not know whether they had relied on his סימן or on his טביעות עין as a תלמיד חכם. The גמרא then goes back to a ברייתא: a found גט is returned to the wife if the husband admits it. It worries that the date on the גט could be earlier than the day it was handed over, letting her take produce from buyers unfairly. It answers that she must prove when she received the גט. A found שטר חוב is not returned with this fix, because a buyer would assume the court already checked its date. The same worry and the same answer are applied to a found bill of freedom for a slave. Next, a ברייתא defines a will and a deed of gift, and אביי explains which gift of a healthy person works like a deathbed gift. Finally, the גמרא points out a contradiction about returning documents when the writer agrees, and רבי אבא בר ממל begins an answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A lost גט is returned to רבה בר בר חנה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה lost a גט in the בית מדרש. He claimed it with both a סימן and טביעות עין, and it was returned to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He lost a גט in the study hall. He said: 'If you want a סימן, I have one for it. If you want טביעות עין, I have that for it too.' They gave it back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about a lost גט that was returned to the person carrying it. He gave two different kinds of proof that it was his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to claim a lost object. A סימן is a specific identifying detail. טביעות עין means 'I just recognize it.' Because he offered both, the בית מדרש's reason for returning the גט is unclear, and the next step depends on exactly that.

steps.title: He is unsure why they returned it
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה says he does not know which proof they relied on. It could have been the סימן, if they hold סימנין דאורייתא. It could have been the טביעות עין, which only works for a צורבא מרבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'I do not know whether they returned it to me because of the סימן, meaning they hold that סימנין work by Torah law. Or maybe they returned it because of my טביעות עין, and that only works for a Torah scholar, not for an ordinary person.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה admits that the story cannot settle the question. We cannot tell which kind of proof the בית מדרש accepted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the סימן was the reason, then סימנין are trusted מדאורייתא, which matters a lot for returning a גט. If the טביעות עין was the reason, the story proves nothing about סימנין, because only a תלמיד חכם is trusted to say 'I recognize it.' So the question about סימנין stays open.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the story proves that סימנין work. רבה בר בר חנה himself says it might have been his טביעות עין as a תלמיד חכם.

steps.title: Back to the ברייתא about finding a גט in the market
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to a ברייתא quoted earlier. If the husband admits the גט, return it to the wife. If he does not admit it, return it to neither of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the matter itself: if someone found a woman's גט in the market and the husband admits it, it should be returned to the wife. If the husband does not admit it, it should not be returned to either one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses 'גופא' to go back and study a ברייתא that was mentioned earlier. It quotes the ברייתא to set up a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling depends on whether the husband agrees that he wrote and gave the גט. If he agrees, the wife gets it and the divorce stands. If he does not agree, the finder holds on to it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A found גט goes to the wife if the husband admits it. Otherwise it goes to no one.

steps.title: Worry that the wife will use an early date to take back sold produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges returning the גט to the wife. Maybe the גט was written in ניסן but only given in תשרי. The husband may have sold the produce in between, and the wife could use the ניסן date to take it back from the buyers unfairly.
steps.simpleTranslation: At least when the husband admits it, the ברייתא says to return it to the wife. But we should worry: maybe he wrote it to give in ניסן but did not give it until תשרי. Meanwhile the husband sold the produce between ניסן and תשרי. Then she shows the גט dated ניסן and comes to take the produce from the buyers unfairly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we can give a found גט to the wife. Its date might not match the day it was actually handed over, and that could cheat buyers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband has rights to the produce of his wife's property until she is divorced. If the גט shows an earlier date than the real handover, the wife could claim the husband sold produce that was no longer his. She would then take it back from buyers who bought it fairly. The husband's admission now does not tell us when he actually gave the גט.

steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a found גט is returned to the wife when the husband admits it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The date on the גט may be earlier than the real handover. The wife could then wrongly take produce from buyers who bought from the husband during that gap.

steps.title: The worry only works for one opinion about the husband's rights
steps.stepSummary: If a husband loses his produce rights once he decides to divorce, the wife takes the produce back fairly. But according to the view that he keeps the rights until he actually hands over the גט, the problem remains.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says that once he decides to divorce her, the husband no longer has rights to the produce. But for the one who says the husband has rights to the produce until the moment he gives the גט, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows its challenge. It shows the problem is real only for one opinion, and asks how the ברייתא works according to that opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the first view, the husband lost his rights back in ניסן when he decided to divorce. So the wife's claim against the buyers is correct, and there is no problem. Under the second view, the husband kept his rights until תשרי. So she would be taking the produce unfairly. The next step answers this.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the husband kept his rights until תשרי, the wife's use of the ניסן date takes produce from buyers unfairly. So returning the גט to her causes harm.
steps.whyThisMatters: The answer to this question will explain why returning a found גט is safe even according to the stricter view of the husband's rights.

steps.title: She must prove when she received the גט
steps.stepSummary: Returning the גט is safe, because when the wife comes to take the produce back from buyers, she must first prove when the גט reached her.
steps.simpleTranslation: When she comes to take back the produce, we tell her: bring proof of when the גט came into your hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from steps 4 and 5. The early date written on the גט won't hurt the buyers, because the wife will have to prove when she actually received it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the wife would use the ניסן date to take produce the husband sold before he actually gave the גט in תשרי. The answer: the date on the גט alone is not enough to collect. She needs proof of the delivery date, and that protects the buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: to take back property that was sold to buyers
proof
when

steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical safeguard: an extra proof is required at the time she collects
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Returning the גט lets the wife collect unfairly from buyers based on its early date.
steps.terutzMaskana: The גט can be returned, because she cannot collect from buyers without proving when she received it.

steps.title: Comparing to lost loan documents
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a found שטר חוב is treated differently. The משנה says not to return it, because of the same early-date worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from loan documents? The משנה says: if someone found loan documents that include a property guarantee, he should not return them. We explained that this is even when the borrower admits the debt. The reason is that maybe the document was written for a loan in ניסן, but the money was only lent in תשרי. Then the lender could unfairly take property from people who bought it in between.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה about lost loan documents that seems to have the exact same problem as the גט. This sets up a challenge: why didn't we use the same 'bring proof' fix there?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the שטר חוב case, the משנה forbids returning it, even when the borrower admits he owes. The only reason is the risk of an early date being used against buyers. That is the very same risk we just solved for the גט by requiring proof, so the two rulings look inconsistent.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The שטר חוב has the same early-date risk, yet the משנה refuses to return it. That suggests the 'bring proof' fix is not accepted.

steps.title: Then return loan documents too
steps.stepSummary: If proof of delivery solves the problem for a גט, the שטר חוב should also be returned, with the lender required to prove when he got it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, let it be returned. When the lender comes to collect from buyers, let us tell him: bring proof of when the loan document came into your hand!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge. By the logic of step 6, the משנה should have allowed returning the שטר חוב as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same safeguard could easily be applied to the lender. He would have to prove when he received the document before taking from buyers. Since the משנה does not do this, the גמרא needs to explain the difference.

steps.kashyaTarget: The difference between the rulings for the גט and the שטר חוב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The step 6 safeguard works just as well for a lender, so there should be no reason to refuse to return the שטר חוב.

steps.title: The buyer knows why the גט was returned
steps.stepSummary: With a גט, the buyer understands the court returned it only so the woman would not be an עגונה. So he will demand proof of the delivery date before she takes from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: here, with a woman's גט, the buyer will come and demand proof from her. He will say: the רבנן returned the גט to her only so she would not be left stuck as an עגונה. Now that she wants to take property from me, let her go and bring proof of when the גט reached her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the 'bring proof' safeguard really works for a גט. The buyer himself will know to demand the proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The safeguard only works if the buyer actually thinks to demand proof. With a גט, the buyer knows there was a separate reason to return it: so she could remarry. That return tells him nothing about her right to collect, so he will insist on proof. The answer implies that with a שטר חוב the buyer has no such reason in mind, so he might not think to demand proof, and the risk remains.

keyTerms.meaning: they say, introducing the answer

steps.confusionAlert: The buyer is not saying the גט is invalid. The גט works for the divorce. He is only saying its return does not prove when she received it for collecting produce.

steps.title: Why the buyer will not ask for proof with a returned שטר חוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the contrast from Step 9. With a returned שטר חוב, the buyer assumes the court returned it so the lender could collect. So he believes the court already confirmed the date, and he does not demand proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here, with a promissory note, the buyer will not come and demand proof. He will say: 'Since the רבנן returned the note to him, it is obvious why. What else would they return it for? It is to collect with it. So the רבנן must have looked into it, and the note reached the lender before I bought the land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes its answer from Step 9. It explains the other half of the contrast: why the buyer does NOT ask for proof when a שטר חוב is returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שטר חוב has only one use, collecting money. So the buyer thinks a court that returned it must have approved collecting from the date written in it, and he gives up his land without a fight. With a גט, the buyer knows it was returned only to free the woman from being an עגונה, so he still demands proof of the delivery date. That is why a found גט is returned and a found שטר חוב is not.

steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes the answer to the challenge in Steps 7–8. Returning a document is safe only if the people it could hurt will still protect themselves by asking for proof.

steps.title: A found bill of freedom: the ברייתא's rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה, found bills of freedom for slaves. It brings a ברייתא: if the master admits he gave it, return it to the slave. If not, return it to neither.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Bills of freeing slaves, etc.' The רבנן taught: If someone found a bill of freedom in the marketplace, and the master admits he gave it, return it to the slave. If the master does not admit it, do not return it to either one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic from the משנה, a found שטר שחרור. It quotes a ברייתא that gives the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the master agrees he freed the slave, there is no argument, so the document goes to the slave. When the master denies it, the finder cannot decide between them. He gives it to neither one. This rule sets up the challenge in the next step.

steps.title: Why return it? The backdated bill of freedom worry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the bill is returned even when the master admits it. Maybe it was written in ניסן but only given in תשרי. The slave could then use the early date to take back property the master sold in between.
steps.simpleTranslation: At least when the master admits, the ברייתא says to return it to the slave. But why? Let us worry that maybe he wrote it in ניסן, planning to give it then, but did not give it until תשרי. Meanwhile the slave bought property between ניסן and תשרי, and the master sold that property. Now the slave shows the bill written in ניסן and takes the property back from the buyers unfairly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. It raises the same early-date worry it used for the גט and the שטר חוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While someone is still a slave, whatever he buys belongs to his master, so the master may sell it. If freedom really began only in תשרי, the master's sales between ניסן and תשרי were legal. But the slave could show the ניסן date to claim the property was his. That would take land from the buyers wrongly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of the ברייתא quoted in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a found שטר שחרור is returned to the slave when the master admits it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The written date may be earlier than the real delivery. The slave could use that earlier date to take property from buyers who bought legally from the master.

steps.title: No problem if freedom starts at the signing
steps.stepSummary: The worry goes away if freedom is a benefit for the slave. Then, as אביי says, the witnesses acquire the document for him as soon as they sign it. The slave is free from the date written, so the ניסן date is true.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well according to the one who says that going free from his master is a benefit for the slave. Together with אביי, who says that the witnesses acquire the document for him through their signatures, the ברייתא is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the challenge has an answer according to one view. This is a setup, because the next step will ask about the other view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You may acquire something for a person without him, if it is good for him. If freedom is good for the slave, the signing witnesses acquire the bill for him right away, in ניסן. So he really was free from ניסן, the property he bought was his, and his claim against the buyers is fair.

keyTerms.meaning: A benefit, something good for the person
Its witnesses, by signing, acquire the document on his behalf
Freedom
This works well (according to a certain view)
אביי, the אמורא whose rule about signing witnesses is quoted here

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says
it is a benefit for the slave
that he goes out from under his master to freedom,
and according to Abaye, who says:
its witnesses, by their signatures, acquire it for him,
it is fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר זְכוּת הוּא לָעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12, but only according to one view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Partial answer that works for only one opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Freedom starts only when the bill is handed over, so the ניסן date is misleading.
steps.terutzMaskana: If freedom is a benefit, the witnesses acquire the bill for the slave at the signing. He is truly free from the written date, so there is no unfair collection.

steps.title: But what if freedom is a disadvantage for the slave?
steps.stepSummary: According to the view that freedom is a disadvantage for the slave, the witnesses cannot acquire it for him. He would be free only when he receives the bill. So the backdating worry comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to the one who says that going free from his master is a disadvantage for the slave, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא presses its challenge against the other view. On that view the answer of Step 13 does not work. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You cannot acquire something for a person without him if it hurts him. If freedom counts as a loss for the slave, the witnesses' signing does nothing for him. He becomes free only at delivery in תשרי. Then the worry from Step 12 is back: why return the bill?

keyTerms.meaning: Here it means a disadvantage, something bad for the person
What is there to say? (The גמרא is asking for an answer)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up חוב here with שטר חוב. Here חוב means 'a disadvantage' (the opposite of זכות), not a debt.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says
it is a disadvantage for the slave
that he goes out from under his master to freedom,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר חוֹב הוּא לָעֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answer of Step 13 works for only one view, and challenges the other view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule according to the view that freedom is a disadvantage for the slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If freedom is a disadvantage, the witnesses cannot acquire the bill for him. Freedom starts only at delivery, so the early written date could again be used to take property from buyers unfairly.

steps.title: The slave must prove when he received the bill
steps.stepSummary: The backdating worry is removed. When the slave comes to take back property, the court tells him to prove when the bill of freedom actually reached his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because when he comes to take back property, we tell him: bring proof of when the bill of freedom reached your hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 14. Even if freedom is a disadvantage for the slave, returning the bill does no harm, because the slave cannot collect by its written date alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the slave would use the early ניסן date to take back property the master sold before תשרי. The answer is that the date on the bill does not decide this. The slave must bring proof of the day he actually received it, so the buyers are protected.

keyTerms.meaning: to repossess, to take property back from a buyer
bring proof
freedom; here, the bill of freedom

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why the ברייתא can say to return the bill when the master admits it, even according to the view that freedom is a disadvantage for the slave.

phrases.english: Because when he comes to repossess
phrases.notes: "He" is the slave, trying to take back property the master sold.

phrases.english: we say to him:
Bring proof
of when the bill of freedom reached your hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Procedural safeguard: the burden of proof is on the slave
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Returning the bill would let the slave use a false early date to take back sold property.
steps.terutzMaskana: The slave must prove when he received the bill, so its written date cannot hurt the buyers.

steps.title: Defining a will and a deed of gift
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה, found wills and gift documents. A ברייתא defines a דייתיקי as a document giving property at death, and a מתנה as a document that says 'from today and after death.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה mentioned wills and gifts. The רבנן taught: what is a דייתיקי? A document saying: 'This will stand and exist so that if he dies, his property goes to so-and-so.' A gift is any document that says 'from today and after death.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: the משנה's case of found wills and gift documents. It brings a ברייתא that defines these two kinds of documents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A דייתיקי is a will: the property passes only if and when the owner dies. A מתנה, according to the ברייתא, is a document written 'from today and after death.' This definition will be questioned in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a will; a document giving property at death
a gift; here, a deed of gift
the רבנן taught (introduces a ברייתא)
from today and after death

phrases.english: Wills, gifts, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: if you find wills or gift documents, you do not return them.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
What is a will?
"This shall be to stand and to exist
phrases.notes: These are the words written in the will itself. The letters of דייתיקי sound like דא תהא, "this shall be."

phrases.english: that if he dies, his property goes to so-and-so."
A gift: any document in which is written
"from today and after death."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה after the slave's bill of freedom
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A דייתיקי gives property if the owner dies; a מתנה is a document written 'from today and after death.'

steps.title: Does a gift only work with 'after death'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the ברייתא seems to say a gift works only if it says 'from today and after death.' Does that mean a plain gift does not work?
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems that only if it says 'from today and after death' does he acquire, and if not, he does not acquire?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's definition of a gift. Read simply, it suggests a gift without those words would not work at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא described a מתנה as a document with the words 'from today and after death.' But a normal gift given simply 'from today' surely works. So the ברייתא cannot mean that only this wording makes a gift valid.

keyTerms.meaning: apparently, so it seems
he acquires

phrases.english: Apparently, if it is written
"from today and after death," that is when he acquires,
and if not, he does not acquire?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא אִי כְּתִיבָא מֵהַיּוֹם וּלְאַחַר מִיתָה הוּא דְּקָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the definition of מתנה in Step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's definition of a מתנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The definition implies that a gift without 'after death' wording is not valid, which cannot be true.

steps.title: אביי: a healthy person's gift that works like a deathbed gift
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains the ברייתא: it is not defining every gift. It is describing which gift of a healthy person works like a deathbed gift, acquired only after death. That is a document saying 'from today and after death.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: this is what it means. Which gift of a healthy person is like the gift of a person on his deathbed, where the receiver acquires only after death? Any document that says 'from today and after death.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by rereading the ברייתא. It is talking about one special kind of gift, not about all gifts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is not saying a gift needs the words 'after death' to be valid. It is saying that when a healthy person writes 'from today and after death,' the gift is like a שכיב מרע's gift: the receiver acquires only after death. A plain gift 'from today' still works as usual.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what it means (rereading a source)
gift of a healthy person
a person on his deathbed

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's 'from today and after death' gift is a special case: a healthy person's gift that works like a deathbed gift, acquired only after death. It does not mean ordinary gifts need this wording.

phrases.english: Abaye said: this is what it is saying:
What is a gift of a healthy person
that is like the gift of a person on his deathbed,
where he acquires only after death?
Any document in which is written "from today and after death."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 17 by rereading the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא defines every valid gift as one written 'from today and after death.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא describes only a healthy person's gift that works like a deathbed gift, acquired after death.

steps.title: Inference from the משנה: if the writer says 'give', we give
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the משנה that the only reason found wills and gifts are not handed over is that the writer never said 'give.' If he did say 'give', the finder hands them over.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason we don't give is that he didn't say 'Give.' But if he said 'Give', we give.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads a hidden rule out of the משנה about found wills and gift documents. It is setting this rule up so that it can be challenged in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said we don't give these documents to the receiver because maybe the writer changed his mind. The גמרא concludes that this worry exists only when the writer is silent. If the writer tells us to give it, the worry is gone, so we hand it over.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason; the גמרא is pointing to the reason behind a rule
But this case; the opposite case, which teaches the opposite rule
Give! (the writer's instruction to hand the document over)
We give; the finder hands it over

phrases.english: The reason is that he did not say 'Give.'
phrases.notes: 'He' is the person who wrote the will or gift document. The משנה worried he might have changed his mind.

phrases.english: But if he said 'Give', we give.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה about found wills and gift documents and draws a new inference from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the writer instructs 'give', the found will or gift document is handed to the receiver.

steps.title: A ברייתא says never return, even if both sides agree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if someone found wills, אפותיקי documents or gift documents, he returns them to neither side, even if both sides agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the גמרא raises a contradiction: if one found wills, אפותיקי documents or gift documents, even if both of them agree, he should not return the document to this one or to that one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the inference from step 19 with a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the משנה we learned that once the writer agrees ('give'), we hand the document over. The ברייתא says that even when the writer and the receiver both agree, the finder gives it to nobody. So the writer's agreement does not seem to help.

keyTerms.meaning: And they pointed out a contradiction between two sources
A document that sets aside a specific property for paying a debt
Agree; admit

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
If one found wills, designated-property documents and gift documents,
even though both of them agree,
phrases.notes: 'Both of them' means the person who wrote the document and the person who is supposed to receive it.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַחְזִיר לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה!
phrases.english: he should return it neither to this one nor to that one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference just drawn from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that the document is handed over if the writer says 'give'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the document is returned to no one, even when both sides agree. So the writer's agreement should not be enough.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying the finder keeps the document for himself. It only says he does not hand it to either side.

steps.title: רבי אבא בר ממל: there is no contradiction
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר ממל begins his answer by saying the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא is not a real problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר ממל said: It is not difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא בר ממל announces that he can resolve the contradiction. This line sets up his answer, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא קשיא' tells us that both sources will stand. The answer will show that the משנה and the ברייתא are talking about different situations. The details have not come yet.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who answers the contradiction
It is not difficult; the two sources do not really clash

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Memel said:
It is not difficult,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל: לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the contradiction in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (the details come on the next amud)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the משנה and the ברייתא disagree about the writer's agreement.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sources are correct. The full explanation comes next.
